list.listitem: Consider insulinoma in patients who have an overnight fasting glucose level of less than 45 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L) and symptoms of hypoglycemia that are relieved by glucose. C
Confirm diagnosis with serum insulin, proinsulin, high C-peptide, and low beta-hydroxybutyrate levels. C
Preoperative localization of the insulinoma should be performed using CT, MRI, endoscopic ultrasound, and/or selective pancreatic arterial calcium stimulation. C
The definitive treatment is surgical. B

background.definition: Insulinoma is a tumor of the pancreatic beta cells that causes an excessive amount of insulin to be produced exclusive of the normal regulatory feedback mechanisms controlling insulin production.

list.listitem: Insulinomas are very rare and occur in 0.5 to 5 persons/1,000,000/y. A systematic review reported a lifetime incidence of 0.4%.
Insulinomas usually occur in patients between the ages of 20 and 75 years, with the majority diagnosed in patients between the ages of 40 and 50 years.
The incidence is somewhat higher in men.
Insulinomas are produced by insulin-secreting tumors in the pancreas.
Insulinomas are the most common of the islet-cell tumors (50%). They are usually benign, solitary, and evenly distributed throughout the pancreas.
Most insulinomas are small; 90% are smaller than 2 cm.
Approximately 10% of insulinomas are malignant.
Ten percent are multiple, and are usually associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.
Sites of ectopic insulinoma (outside the pancreas) included duodenum, jejunum, stomach, and female reproductive organs.

Patients with insulinoma commonly present with Whipple's triad: signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia, a median blood glucose level of less than 40 mg/dL, and relief of symptoms with glucose administration. C
If an overnight fast confirms hypoglycemia (<45 mg/dL or 2.5 mmol/L) confirm with exercise test, prolonged fasting test, mixed meal test, or glucose reduction challenge. C
Low plasma glucose, high serum insulin, high C-peptide, or low beta-hydroxybutyrate levels should warrant further studies to localize insulinoma. C
Preoperative localization of the insulinoma should be performed using one of various imaging modalities (CT, MRI, endoscopic ultrasound, or selective pancreatic arterial calcium stimulation). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Endogenous antibodies attack insulin and the insulin receptor
Usually in neonates and young children

list.listitem: Almost all patients with insulinoma present with Whipple's triad which is: clinical signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia, overnight fasting blood glucose of less than 45 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L), and relief of symptoms with glucose administration.

Neuroglycopenic symptoms may present acutely, subacutely, or chronically. Acute symptoms include sweating, anxiety, tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, and diaphoresis. Subacute symptoms present as episodic disorientation, somnolence, and personality changes. Chronic symptoms are rare, but may resemble schizophrenia or personality disorder.
The hypoglycemia usually occurs several hours after a meal and resolves shortly after ingestion of glucose containing foods.

In a series of 15 patients with malignant insulinoma at a Chinese center, half had metastases on presentation, most commonly to liver (87%), local tissues (33%) and abdominal lymph nodes (13%). All had neuroglycopenic or autonomic symptoms.
Tests useful for diagnosis of insulinoma include an overnight fast test, an exercise test, a prolonged fasting test, a mixed meal test, and a glucose reduction challenge.

The initial test is usually an overnight fast: positive test is plasma glucose 45 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L) after overnight fast of 18 hours on 3 separate occasions. If abnormal, further testing is warranted.

A systematic review found 2 case-control studies with 106 comparing the accuracy of insulin and c-peptide measured during an oral glucose tolerance test were 87% sensitive and 95% specific for diagnosis of insulinoma.

Exercise test: serum glucose levels are drawn 10 minutes before exercise, every 10 minutes during intense exercise and 30 minutes after intense exercise. Plasma insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin levels are increased with endogenous hyperinsulinemia.

Prolonged fasting test: performed over 48 hours in a controlled setting under medical supervision. Patients are allowed to drink noncaloric, caffeine free beverages during the fast, and are encouraged to ambulate while awake. Blood is drawn every 6 hours until plasma glucose is 65 mg/dL (3.5 mmol/L), then every 1 to 2 hours. The fast is terminated after adequate specimen collection, when glucose is less than 45 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L), and neuroglycopenic symptoms are present. The patient is fed at the end of the test. In the absence of symptoms and hypoglycemia the test is stopped at 48 hours.

Mixed meal test: The mixed meal test is used to check postprandial neuroglycopenic symptoms. No standard protocols are set, and the patient should eat a meal similar to the one which caused the symptoms. Arterial samples are drawn every 30 minutes for 6 hours after the meal. The test is considered positive if neuroglycopenic symptoms are present along with glucose measurements of less than 55 mg/dL (3 mmol/L). Venous blood is not used because glucose may be 15 to 30 mg/dL (1-2 mmol/L) lower than arterial blood.

Glucose reduction challenge: In the glucose reduction challenge patients are given insulin IV for 3 hours at 40 mU/kg/h. Plasma glucose will drop to less than 2.5 mmol/L in patients with insulinoma but will generally remain at greater than 45 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L) in patients without insulinoma.

After biochemical analysis, various imaging studies are used for preoperative localization to determine surgical approach. Imaging techniques include CT, MRI, and endoscopic ultrasound and have varying sensitivities. In one series, sensitivity was 79% for CT, 85% for MRI, and 95% for EUS. A systematic review of endoscopic ultrasound for insulinoma localization identified 9 studies with 350 patients. There was good homogeneity and the summary estimates of accuracy were sensitivity 81%, specificity 90%, LR+ 7.9, LR- 0.21.
A systematic review of 19 studies with 708 patients compared imaging strategies for localization. PET/CT was 79% sensitive and 84% specific, while MRI was 54% sensitive and 65% specific.

Other tests used to localize insulinoma include selective pancreatic arterial calcium stimulation, endoscopic ultrasound, and intraoperative ultrasound.Adding pancreatic perfusion to CT improves its accuracy.
Patients typically present with Whipple's triad: signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia, median blood glucose of less than 40 mg/dL, and relief of symptoms with administration of glucose.
When evaluating the patient with hypoglycemia, always consider accidental or intentional injection of insulin or excessive sulfonylureas.
If overnight fasting blood glucose is less than 45 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L), consider insulinoma and obtain a prolonged fast test, exercise test, mixed meal test, or glucose reduction challenge.
If any of the previous tests are positive, obtain imaging studies (CT, MRI, or endoscopic ultrasound).
Large insulinomas and patients with a c-peptide value >6.1 ng/ml are more likely to have a malignant tumor.
Once the tumor is localized, a surgical consult should be obtained to determine whether laparoscopic or open surgery is best for removal of the tumor.
Definitive treatment for insulinomas is surgery. Laparoscopic surgery is as effective as open surgery. B
Diazoxide, octreotide, streptozocin, doxorubicin, and somatostatin can help control symptoms prior to surgery. B
Newer modalities of treatment are being researched and show promise for the 5% to 15% of insulinomas that are metastatic. C

Drug therapy is primarily for symptom relief. The mainstay of palliative drug therapy is diazoxide, which increases blood glucose by inhibiting insulin release from the pancreas. Fluid status and platelet counts require careful monitoring. Other medications that can be used are verapamil, diphenylhydantoin, and octreotide.

Somatostatin can improve symptoms by inhibiting the release of vasoactive amines and peptides. Radiolabeled analogs of somatostatin are also used to help with identification of lesions prior to surgery.
Chemotherapeutic agents such as streptozotocin, doxorubicin, dacarbazine, or interferon-B may also help improve symptoms.
111In-octreotide therapy is being studied for effectiveness in symptom relief, and has shown a 66% response rate in early trials.

Surgical therapy is the only potentially curative treatment available at this time. Laparoscopic surgery seems to be as effective as open surgery, and patients leave the hospital earlier after the laparoscopic procedure with lower mortality.
The surgical procedure to be performed is determined by preoperative localization of the tumor.

The types of surgical procedures include pancreatic enucleation, distal pancreatectomy with splenic preservation, or pancreatoduodenectomy. Procedures may be performed laproscopically or as open surgery.
A case series described successful endoscopic ultrasound guided ethanol ablation in 4 patients.

A systematic review identified 8 studies with 150 patients reporting the outcome of endoscopic ultrasound guided ablation (EUSA) and 9 studies with 236 patients reporting outcomes of minimally invasive surgery (MIS). Patients in the EUSA group were older (64 vs 45 years). Technical success (100% for EUSA, 97% for MIS) and clinical success (99% for MIS, 94% for EUSA) were generally similar. Patients undergoing EUSA had a shorter hospital stay but this is health system dependent.

A systematic review of observational studies and case series identified 19 reports with 183 patients treated with endoscopic ultrasound guided radiofrequency ablation for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. The adverse event rate was 18% and the clinical efficacy rate was 95% for functional tumors.
Open procedures are preferred for tumors that are malignant, multiple, located on the posterior wall, or deep in the head of the pancreas.
Debulking of metastases by surgery or embolization may improve symptoms.
When the diagnosis is made, a surgical consult should be obtained to determine the possibility of resection.
Prognosis is good for insulinomas; the majority of patients remain disease free after surgery. B
Factors that predict malignancy include greater age, elevated insulin or C-peptide levels, and increasing tumor size.B
